text: ## ACCIDENTAL DEATHS A total of 108987 accidental deaths were recorded by the police in the country during 1979 against 118594 accidental deaths recorded in 1978 registering a decline of 8·1 percent in 1979 over 1978. Figures recorded in 1979 are also lower than the figures recorded during the last 5 years i.e. from 1974 to 1978. ## Volume of Accidental Deaths per lakh of population

## ALL INDIA SURVEY During 1969, 1,30,755 deaths were reported in India, which had resulted from accidents of various types. The causes of accidents have been classified into two broad categories viz., (i) Accidents due to acts of nature such as snake bites/animal killing, floods, land-slides etc. and (ii) Accidents due to other causes such as mishappenings in factories, air-crashes, railway accidents etc. The detailed break-up of such accidental deaths in the country due to various causes is furnished in Table I. This Table shows that deaths due to acts of nature account for 29.0% deaths and those due to other causes constitute the remaining 71.0% of the total accidental deaths in the country. Drowning accounted for the highest number of cases (27,079) constituting 20.7% of the total. Animal bite/killing caused deaths in 4,965 cases, while road, railway and fire accidents accounted for 5.4%, 6.0% and 6.9% respectively of total accidental deaths in the country. The pattern of percentage distribution of accidental deaths due to various causes has been more or less the same as during 1966, 1967 and 1968 except for drowning and road accidents. The percentage of deaths on the road has been 5.4 during 1969 as against 4.8 during 1968. The percentage of deaths due to drowning has decreased from 23.1 in 1968 to 20.7 in 1969. TABLE I

## ALL INDIA SURVEY During the year 1971, 43,675 suicides were reported in India as against 48,428 during 1970, indicating a decrease of 9·8%. Table 6 presents the comparative incidence of suicidal deaths during the period 1964 to 1971. The incidence of suicides has been increasing from 1965 to 1970 but in 1971 it indicated a very sharp decrease. The volume of suicides per one lakh of population has also increased from 6·3 during 1965 to 8·8 during 1970, but in 1971 it decreased to 7·9. On an average more than 60·3% of the total suicides were committed by males while persons in the age-group of 18 to 30 years were more prone to commit suicides. This age-group accounted for 44·7% of the total suicides in the country during 1971. TABLE-VI

## ALL-INDIA SURVEY During 1968, 1,26,232 deaths were reported in India which had resulted from accidents of various types. The causes of accidents have been classified into two broad categories viz. (i) Accidents due to acts of nature such as snake bite, animal killing, floods, land-slides etc. and (ii) Accidents due to other causes such as mishaps in factories, air crashes, railway accidents etc. The detailed break-up of such accidental deaths in the country due to various causes is furnished in Table I. This Table shows that deaths due to acts of nature accounted for 26·9% of the total accidental deaths. Railway accidents and accidents on the roads accounted for 6·3% and 4·8% of the total accidental deaths respectively. Quite a substantial number of persons (4,581)died because of animal bite/killing. The most prominent accidental killer was drowning accounting for 23·1% of all such deaths. The pattern of the percentage distribution of accidental deaths due to various causes is more or less the same as during 1966 and 1967, except that deaths due to poisoning registered a sharp rise of about 37% over 1967. This constituted 6·3% of the total accidental deaths during 1968 as against 4·7% and 4·2% during 1966 and 1967 respectively. TABLE I

## All-India Survey During 1967, 1,26,762 deaths were reported in India which had resulted from accidents. Out of this total 36,313 deaths (28·7% of the total incidence) were due to acts of nature such as snake-bites, floods, land-slides, lightning, heat-strokes and others. 90,449 cases (71·3% of the total incidence) were due to other forms of accidents such as those on roads, those due to air crashes and others resulting from mishappenings in factories, railways etc. Table I presents the actual and percentage incidence of accidental deaths during 1967 due to various causes. It has been observed that the most prominent accidental killer was drowning (24·7% of total deaths due to all causes together). Accidents on roads and railways accounted for 4·9% and 5·6% of deaths respectively. Fire and animal bites/killing were responsible for 6·5% and 3·5% of deaths respectively. The pattern of percentage distribution of incidence due to various causes is more or less the same as during 1965 and 1966. TABLE—1

## PART—II ## SUICIDES IN INDIA A total of 54,357 suicides were reported in India during 1986 compared to 52,811 in 1985 registering an increase of 2.9% in 1986 over 1985. The numerical increase registered during 1986 over 1985 was of 1,546 suicidal deaths. The total number of suicidal deaths in India recorded in 1986 was an all-time high during the period of 11 years since 1976.

## SUICIDES A total of 38217 suicides were reported in India during 1979 compared with the figure of 40207 in 1978 registering a decline of 4.9 percent in 1979 over 1978. The numerical decline registered during 1979 over 1978 was 1990. Incidentally the number of suicides in 1979 was the lowest in any one year since 1972. During the period 1972—79, the trend in suicide cases has been erratic. It is seen from the suicide figures that during the period of 8 years, the highest number of suicides was recorded during 1974 (46008) with a volume of 7.8 per lakh of population. If we see the volume only, the figures generally showed a downward trend except for 1974 but the actual number of suicides tell a different story as against 43601 suicides in 1972 it came down to 40807 in 1973 and again went up to 46008 in 1974. It came down continuously for three years again during 1975 to 1977 but went up again in 1978 to 40207 and came down to the lowest number in 1979 (38217). 10 ## Union Territories : The incidence of accidental deaths went up to 1.5 percent in 1980 over 1979 in the Union Territories as a whole while a decline of 3.6 percent was recorded in 1979 over 1978. The Union Territories which registered a decline in the total number of accidental deaths in 1980 over 1979 were, Mizoram (30.4%), Pondicherry (1.8%), and Goa, Daman & Diu (1.7%) and the Union Territories which registered an increase were Arunachal Pradesh (34.5%), Chandigarh (29.0%), Dadra & Nagar Haveli (28.6%), Andaman & Nicobar Islands (9.7%) and Delhi (1.3%). In Lakshadweep 5 cases of accidental deaths were reported in year 1980 as against nil in 1979.

10 ## Union Territories The incidence of accidental deaths came down to 9·2 per cent in 1983 over 1982 in the Union Territories as a whole. The Union Territories, which registered a decline in the total number of accidental deaths in 1983 over 1982 were Lakshadweep (33·3%), A & N Islands (10·0%), Chandigarh (6·4%) and Delhi (5·8%). Rest of the U.Ts. registered an increase in total number of accidental deaths over 1982.

15 ## ALL-INDIA SURVEY During the year 1969, 43,633 suicides were reported in India as against 40,688 during 1968, indicating an increase of 7.2%. Table 6 presents the comparative incidence of suicides during the last 6 years. It may be observed that the trend in suicides is consistently on an increase from 1965 onwards, i.e. it increased from 30,669 cases during 1965 to 43,633 cases during 1969. The volume of suicides i.e. per one lakh of population also increased from 6.3 during 1965 to 8.1 during 1969. The volume of suicides registered by the rest of the States was less than 10.00. The lowest volume of suicides was recorded by Bihar (0.48) and Jammu & Kashmir (0.86). Among the Metropolitan Cities, Madras topped the list with a Volume of 21.65 suicides per lakh of population followed by Bangalore (18.74) and Nagpur (13.22), while it was the lowest in Calcutta (3.75). 19 ## INCIDENCE OF SUICIDAL DEATHS IN THE STATES, UNION TERRITORIES AND CITIES DURING 1971 The regional distribution of suicidal deaths during 1971 showed marked variations from State to State over 1970. The highest increase during 1971 over 1970 was noticed in the State of Gujarat (57·9%) while significant decreases were noticed in Bihar (64·8%) and Uttar Pradesh (34·1%). Among the Union Territories, a substantial number of suicidal deaths were registered in Delhi and Pondicherry and these very Union Territories indicated decreases of 40·8% and 11·3% respectively over 1970. Among the cities, Ahmedabad and Bangalore indicated increases over 1970, the increases being 155·6% and 67·4% respectively, while all other cities under study indicated decreases, a sharp decrease being noticed in Madras 46·4%. The highest number of suicidal deaths were recorded in West Bengal (7.959) followed by Tamil Nadu (5,124), Maharashtra (4,219) and Uttar Pradesh (4,177) and these 4 States together accounted for about 50% of the total suicidal deaths in the entire country. The highest volume of suicidal deaths per one lakh of population was also noticed in West Bengal (17·8) followed by Kerala (15·6), Tripura (12·8). Tamil Nadu (12·4) and Haryana (11·9) as against the All-India average of 7·9. Among the Union Territories the volume of suicidal deaths per one lakh of population was very high in Andaman & Nicobar Islands (55·2), Dadra & Nagar Haveli (28·4), and Pondicherry (46·2).

20 ## Causes of Suicides The total number of suicides reported during 1975 has been classified under different heads and the last category 'other causes' covers the unspecified causes of suicides. The major cause of suicides during 1975 was 'Despair over Dreadful Diseases' (16.4 per cent). The second important cause was 'Quarrel with parents-in law' (9.5 per cent), followed by 'Love Affairs' (6.1 per cent), Quarrel with Spouses (5.9 per cent), 'Poverty' (3.7 per cent), 'Insanity, (2.6 per cent) and 'Failure in examination' (2.3 per cent). The causes comparatively less important were 'dispute over property' (2.1 per cent), 'Unemployment' (1.0 per cent), 'Bankruptcy' (1.0 per cent), 'Deaths of dear persons' (0.8 per cent) and 'Fall in social reputation' (0.7 per cent). The category 'Other causes' accounted for 47.9 per cent of the total suicides registered during 1975. The detailed statistics are presented in Table No. 2.

ACCIDENTAL DEATHS & SUICIDES IN INDIA - 1993 N.C.R.B.- 16 1.3.4 Approximately one-fourth of the total ‘Accidental Deaths’ were reported due to ‘Road Accidents’ during the year, a large majority (91%) of which were due to motor vehicle mishaps. TABLE-3.1 presents the distribution of ‘Motor Vehicles Deaths’ and their rate of occurrence in various States/UTs during the years 1992 & 1993. It is interesting to note that although the number of Motor Vehicles increased by 10.3 per cent in the country during 1992 and by another 7.6 per cent in 1993, the rate of ‘Accidental Deaths’ per thousand ‘Motor Vehicles’ surprisingly decreased by 2.2 and 7.8 per cent respectively during the same period. Contrary to expectations, the highest rate of deaths was reported from hill states of Himachal Pradesh (4.47) and Meghalaya (4.07) which was more than double the National average. The comparatively higher growth in the number of vehicles in the country has, no doubt, contributed to the decline in the above rate of motor vehicle accidents. However other highly correlated factors like growing safety consciousness amongst drivers and pedestrians in obeying traffic regulations, increased electrification and better conditions of the roads, hi-technology checks using computerised periscope vans, radar guns, video traffic monitors etc. coupled with more intensive and extensive monitoring of the vehicular movements by the traffic police are expected to have contributed in the reduction of the accident rate.

ALL INDIA SURVEY During 1970, 1,39,752 deaths were reported in India which had resulted from accidents of various types. The causes of accidents have been classified into two broad categories viz. (i) Accidents due to acts of nature such as animal bites/killing, floods, landslides etc. and (ii) Accidents due to other causes such as mishappenings in factories, aircrashes, railway accidents etc. The details are shown in Appendices I and II. The break-up of such accidental deaths in the entire country due to various causes is furnished in Table I. It may be seen that deaths due to acts of nature account for 30.2% and those due to other causes constitute the remaining 69.8% of the total accidental deaths in the country. As observed in previous years also, drowning accounted for a very large number of deaths (27,915) and constituted 20% of the total. Road accidents and accidents on the railways accounted for 7,288 and 8,282 deaths respectively. The pattern of the percentage distribution of accidental deaths due to various causes has been more or less the same as in the past five years, except for accidents on the roads and deaths due to poisoning. The number of deaths due to poisoning has increased from 8,308 during 1969 to 9,738 during 1970. TABLE-I Incidence of Accidental Deaths in India due to various causes, 1970

ALL INDIA SURVEY During the year 1970, 48,428 suicides were reported in India as against 43,633 during 1969 indicating a very sharp increase of 11.0%. Table VI presents the comparative incidence of suicides during the last 7 years viz. 1964 to 1970. It will be observed that the incidence of suicides is increasing from the year 1965 onwards and the highest increase in any two consecutive years has been noticed during 1969-1970. The volume of suicides per one lakh of population has also increased from 6.3 during 1965 to 8.8 during 1970. The increase in suicides during the period from 1965-1970 was 57.9%, while the increase in population during the same period was 13.0%, indicating thereby that the rate of growth of suicides has been approximately 4 times the rate of growth of population. On an average, 59.6% of the total suicides are committed by males, while persons in the age group of 18 to 30 years are more prone to commit suicide. This age group accounted for 43.5% of the total suicides in the country during 1970. TABLE-VI Comparative Statement of Incidence of Suicides During the Last Seven Years (i.e. 1964 to 1970)

Causes of Accidental Deaths The total accidental deaths recorded during 1982 have been classified under two broad categories: (A). Accidental Death due to natural causes like lighting, heat strokes, floods, land slides, cold and exposure and cyclone, and (B) Accidental deaths due to other causes like mishaps in factoreis, road accidents, air crashes, house collapse and boat capsizing. Category (A) accounted for 3 · 6 per cent of total accidental deaths recorded in 1982 in comparison to 3 · 3 percent in 1981. Under this category, the maximum number of deaths in 1982 were due to ‘Lightning’ (1754) followed by ‘Floods’ (699) ‘Land Slides’ (596), ‘Cyclone’ (505), ‘Heat Strokes’ (492) and ‘Cold & Exposure’ (391). Category (B) claimed 96 · 4 per cent of the total accidental deaths registered during 1982 as against 96 · 7 per cent registered during 1981. Under this category, the highest number of accidental deaths in 1982 was recorded under the head ‘By Drowning’ (22,632), followed by ‘Accidental Death on Roads (22,199), ‘By Fire’ (14,555), ‘In Railways’ (12,789), ‘By poisoning’ (6,846), ‘By snake biting’ (3,299), ‘By fire arms (1,874) ‘By animal biting/killing’ (1,437), ‘By house collapse’ (1,157), ‘In factoreis’ (735), ‘In mines and Quarry Disaster (624), By explosion (356), ‘By boat capsize’ (161) and in ‘Air crashes’ (102). The Miscellaneous causes’ recorded a total number of 32,790 accidental death cases during 1982 as against 31,827 cases in 1981 sharing 26 · 0 per cent of the total accidental deaths. During 1982 ‘Drowning’ accounted for 18 · 0 per cent of the total accidents in India followed by ‘Accidental Death on Roads’ (17 · 6%), ‘By Fire’ (11 · 6%) and in ‘Railways’ (10 · 1%). Incidence of Suicidal Deaths in the States, Union Territories and Cities during 1970 The regional distribution of suicidal deaths shows marked variations from State to State as compared to the previous years and as against the All-India increase of 11.0% during 1970 over 1969. There were higher increases in the States of Andhra Pradesh (18.1%), Bihar (25.9%), Madhya Pradesh (32.4%), Maharashtra (35.3%) and West Bengal (23.6%), while Gujarat (35.1%). Rajasthan (19.8%) registered significant decreases. In the Union Territories, Delhi indicated a significant increase of 55.9%. In the Cities under study, marked decreases of 235.3% and 81.3% were noticed in Bangalore and Kanpur, while Delhi (55.6%), Bombay (39.8%) and Madras (151.7%) showed marked increases during 1970 over the previous year. Wherever marked increases have been noticed over the previous year these were mainly due to 'despair over dreadful diseases' or due to 'other causes.' However, in West Bengal, a large number of suicides was due to failure in examinations and quarrels with parents-in-law contributed a significant increase in the suicidal deaths during 1970 over 1969. The volume of suicides per lakh of population registered an increase from 8.4 in 1969 to 9.1 in 1970. The volume of suicides per lakh of population registered a declining trend till 1973. In 1974, the volume of suicides per lakh of population increased to 7.8 but in 1975 & 1976 it again came down to 7.2 & 6.8, respectively. (ACCIDENTAL DEATHS) Accidental deaths in India, involving national population of over 68 crore people, showed an increase of 3.0 percent during the year 1982, over 1981 while the percentage increase in population figures during 1981 over 1980 was 3.1%. Estimated mid-year population figures for 1982 were not available and in absence of these figures, census figures as on 1-3-1981 have been taken for the calculation of volume of accidental deaths, as well as volume of suicides per lakh of population.
A total of 1,25,993 accidental deaths were recorded by police in the country during 1983 against 1,22,221 accidental deaths recorded in 1981.

This number further came down to 1,08,987 in 1979 but increased continuously up to 1982. From the number 1,16,912 in 1980 it went up to 1,22,221 in 1981 and 1,25,993 in 1982. The variations in the incidence of accidental deaths in the different regions result from a large number of factors peculiar to the region such as the topography of the area, the population, the level of industrialisation and other socio-economic factors. Considering population as one of the major concomitant variants, the volume of accidental deaths per one lakh of population in the different States and Union Territories and Cities has been estimated and presented in Table IV. The highest number of accidental deaths occurred in the State of Maharashtra (24944) followed by Uttar Pradesh (19915), Madhya Pradesh (18207) and West Bengal (12436). These four States together accounted for 54% of total accidental deaths in the entire country. The volume of accidental deaths per one lakh of population was also the highest in Maharashtra (49.7), followed by Madhya Pradesh (44.6), Orissa (35.7), Gujarat (29.1) and West Bengal (27.7) against an average of 25.3 for all the States together. The volume of accidental deaths is consistently higher in all the Union Territories, except Laccadives, the average being 40.1% for all the Union Territories together. Among the Cities, the highest volume of accidental deaths was noticed in Bombay (107.7) and the lowest in Calcutta (12.3) against an average of 53.8 for all the Cities under study together. Though the children’s population (up to 14 years age) as per census 2001 was 30.4 per cent of the total population, children accounted for 9.4 per cent in the proportion of victims of accidental deaths. In general males, accounting for 72.4 per cent of total victims were at a greater risk from accidents than females. Most of the victims of accidents were aged between 15 to 44 years. This group of people constituted nearly two-third (60.4%) of all persons killed in the accidents in the country. Causes of Accidental Deaths The percentage of ‘Accidental Deaths’ due to Natural Causes and those due to Un-Natural Causes were 13.5% and 86.5% respectively. The total deaths due to Accidents increased by 5.9 per cent over the previous year. However, the magnitude of ‘Accidental Deaths’ by Natural Causes increased by (111.1%) and that of deaths by Un-Natural Causes decreased by 1.7 per cent during 2001. The share of deaths due to Natural causes in total accidental deaths increased to 13.5 per cent compared to 6.8 per cent in the previous year. The share of deaths due to natural calamities such as ‘Earthquake’, ‘Avalanche’, ‘Lightning’ and Un- Natural causes such as ‘Collapse of Structure’, ‘Killing by Animals’, ‘Sudden Deaths’, ‘Mines or Quarry disaster’, ‘Falls’, ‘Poisoning’, ‘Factory/Machine Accidents’, ‘Killing by Fire Arms’ and ‘Rail-Road Accidents’ has increased. The same has decreased due to Natural causes such as ‘Flood’, ‘Starvation/Thirst’, ‘Torrential Rain’, ‘Cold & Exposure’, ‘Cyclone/Tornado’ and Un-Natural causes such as ‘Air Crash’, ‘Stampede’, ‘Explosion’, ‘Fire’, ‘Suffocation’, and ‘Drowning’, etc. The average rate of Accidental Deaths has marginally increased from 25.5 in 2000 to 26.4 in 2001 due to increase of rate for all major causes of Accidental Deaths. There was an upward trend to begin with when from 126232 in 1968 the number of accidental deaths increased to 139752 in 1970. After some fall in 1971, there has been a steady increase from 106184 in 1972 to 113016 in 1975. However, the figure of 1975 is lower than the figure of 1968 by 10.5%. Accidental deaths per lakh of population increased in the period 1968-70 from 24.7 to 26.2 while in the period 1971-73 it registered a downward trend & touched 18.5 in 1973. In 1974, it registered a slight increase & stood at 18.9. In 1975 it stood at 18.9.
